strengths: The paper is well-written and clearly structured.
The figures are visually appealing, and the results are reported over a reasonable number of repetitions and with error bars.
The introduction and background section are concise and easy to follow, except maybe for section 3.3, for which additional background is given in the appendix.
Using neural processes for learning imputation models for neural SBI can still be a valuable contribution to the field of SBI.
The derivations for combining imputation models with NPE appear technically sound.
Experimental results support the initial claims that the proposed method is more robust to missing data than the baselines.
I believe the paper is presented quite clearly.

The paper addresses an important problem in the field of SBI, as actual SBI applications usually deal with real-world observations that often have missing data, and it will be a valuable addition to the field if concerns on the evaluation are addressed.

The paper is clearly written and easy to follow; it can be appreciated by both readers familiar with SBI and newcomers to the field. It addresses an important practical problem and is of interest to the community.
The joint training of a posterior surrogate and latent variable missing data model is original, quite general, and useful for SBI applications where the simulator is cheap to run.
The evaluation features a variety of different models (even though the selected four SBI benchmarks are rather uninteresting and not specifically designed to assess the impact of missingness).
The paper tackles a significant and underexplored problem in SBI—handling missing data—and provides a novel solution by jointly learning imputation and inference models.

The authors provide a formal analysis showing how naive imputation leads to biased posterior estimates, strengthening the motivation for their method. The cases for MNAR, MAR, and MCAR have been nicely formalized. The simplification of \(\mathcal{L}_{RISE}\) by \(\mathcal{L}_{NPE}\) in Proposition 2 is particularly convenient.
The method can generalize across varying levels of missing data (RISE-Meta), making it practical for real-world applications.

This work presents the RISE method, which innovatively combines data imputation and neural posterior estimation to address the issue of missing data in SBI. This combination is novel within the SBI domain.
The authors have validated the effectiveness of the method using multiple benchmark models and real-world datasets under various experimental settings.
The paper is well-organized and the figures are easy for readers to understand.
The paper addresses a timely, relevant topic.
Motivation and approach are clearly laid out.
The evaluation spans statistical problems and real world data sets.
RISE outperforms baselines on problems considered.
This paper addresses handling missing data simulation-based inference, which is a common problem in fields like astrophysics.
The experiments include reasonable examples and the results seem to be good.
The method is well motivated by including a probabilistic model over the missingness.
Overall the paper is clear and well structured.
weaknesses: The paper misses discussion of an early SBI paper that addressed imputation in SBI (Lueckmann et al. 2017) and should compare to that work.

The discussion of the work by Gloeckler et al. is not accurate; the Simformer learns imputation of missing data and is very similar to the proposed approach, requiring a more detailed and accurate discussion.
The choice of MMD and RMSE as performance metrics is not ideal; MMD can be misleading depending on kernel bandwidth and RMSE measures parameter discovery rather than posterior accuracy.
It is suggested to also calculate C2ST, the nominal log posterior probability, and evaluate calibration properties such as SBC or expected coverage.
More details are needed on how the training data set for RISE is constructed, including the number of simulations used and simulation budgets for different benchmark tasks.
Comparisons of training time and memory usage of RISE versus baselines should be provided.

The formalization of the problem in SBI is a bit of a stretch, as it is simply the standard missing data setting; propositions are straightforward and there is notational confusion regarding $x_{obs}$.

The method may be overkill for simple data such as the 1D Ricker model; Figure 1 demonstrates bad practice and model misspecification, and limitations for low-dimensional data with simple missingness patterns should be acknowledged.
The paper lacks key ablation studies demonstrating the impact of a bad $p(x_{miss}\mid x_{obs})$ model on posterior variance and calibration.
Calibration error metrics such as expected coverage or probability calibration error should be added to assess reliability of posterior estimates.
The notation needs polishing, e.g., bold font inconsistencies and clarification of scope with respect to different data structures and missingness patterns.
Some citations have inaccuracies, e.g., Gloeckler et al. is an ICML paper, not an arXiv preprint, and the year for Radev et al. is incorrect.
Algorithm 1 should illustrate that the method results in an ensemble of posteriors and that this ensemble uncertainty is integrated out for inference.
Details on simulation budgets for the experiments are missing; performance as a function of simulation budget should be quantified.
Clarity of presentation issues: mathematical formulations and explanations could be clearer; Figure 1 axes are not defined until later sections.
The literature review on handling missing values is limited; traditional techniques such as EM and MICE are not acknowledged.
Computational efficiency is not analyzed; the added complexity of jointly learning the imputation model and the inference network may be costly.
Important limitations such as the Gaussian assumption are not highlighted, despite potential computational infeasibility.
Source code for reproduction is not provided.
The authors report only MMD and RMSE as performance metrics; additional metrics like C2ST, negative log probability of true parameters, and median distances should be included.
Comparisons to simplistic baselines NPE-Zero and NPE-Mean are overly simplistic and introduce bias; more rigorous baselines such as Gloeckler et al. (2024) should be added.
The choice of conditional density estimator (MAFs) over Neural Spline Flows (NSFs) is not justified; an ablation study comparing the two should be provided.
Some comparisons are missing; the HH example would benefit from quantitative evaluation.
Previous literature citations are inaccurate in several places.

The paper should clarify that it focuses on multiple observations or amortized estimation; otherwise, removing missing indices in a single‑observation case is a trivial solution that is not addressed.
The review of previous work is insufficient; relevant methods such as kernel density estimation or nearest‑neighbor imputation are omitted.
The notation with $x_{obs}$ may confuse readers as it is used for both simulated and observed data.
The title is too broad and does not inform about the presented method.
The joint training objective appears separable into independent problems; the paper does not explain why joint training is necessary or beneficial.
No code has been provided to the reviewers.
